message.content:
The largest planet that astronomers have confidently identified so far is **HD 100546 b**. It orbits the young B‑type star HD 100546 (about 320 light‑years away) and has a radius roughly **2.5–3 times that of Jupiter**, making it one of the biggest “hot Jupiters” ever found. Its mass is estimated at around 10–20 Jupiter masses, placing it near the boundary between massive planets and low‑mass brown dwarfs—so its classification sometimes depends on how strictly you draw that line.

Because new exoplanets are being discovered all the time, especially with missions like *TESS* and upcoming telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the record could change. Some candidates that were initially thought to be planets turned out to be brown dwarfs once their true masses were measured. Thus, while HD 100546 b holds the current title among confirmed planetary‑mass objects, the list remains open to revision as our detection techniques improve.
